{
  "primary_meaning": "A miraculous deed, wonder, or token performed by God or His authorized messengers that authenticates divine authority, reveals God's glory or presence, and is intended to produce faith or obedience",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 2:11",
    "John 20:30-31",
    "Acts 2:22",
    "Exodus 4:1-9",
    "Exodus 7:3",
    "Mark 16:17-20",
    "Hebrews 2:4"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Covenantal tokens or memorials that mark God's promises and the people's identity or obligations (e.g., rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, blood on doorposts)",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 9:12-17",
        "Genesis 17:11",
        "Exodus 12:13",
        "Exodus 31:13",
        "Ezekiel 20:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Prophetic or eschatological portents and cosmic indicators of coming judgment, the Day of the Lord, or the return of Christ ('signs of the times')",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 24:3, 24, 30",
        "Luke 21:11, 25",
        "Joel 2:30-31",
        "Acts 2:19",
        "Revelation 12:1, 15:1"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Symbolic prophetic actions or enacted parables that convey a message from God",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 20:3",
        "Ezekiel 4:1-3",
        "Ezekiel 12:6, 11",
        "Jeremiah 13:1-11"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A specific christological pointer, especially the 'sign of Jonah' as prefiguring Jesus' death and resurrection, or the virgin birth as a messianic sign",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 12:38-40",
        "Matthew 16:4",
        "Luke 11:29-30",
        "Isaiah 7:14",
        "Luke 2:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In both Testaments the core semantic range of 'sign' (Heb. ʾôt; Gk. sēmeion) centers on divine authentication and revelation; the miracle/wonder sense is dominant in Christian proclamation and Johannine theology, while covenantal and eschatological uses remain standard and non-contradictory within the broader category. No major Christian tradition redefines the term outside this family of meanings."
}
